intro: RAII is arguably THE central idea of idiomatic C++ resource management — everything in this group is either a direct application of it (smart pointers, PImpl) or the rule-of-thumb machinery around making it work correctly (Rule of Five, exception safety, allocators).

concepts.intro: RAII binds a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime: acquire the resource in the constructor, release it in the destructor. Because C++ *guarantees* that destructors run when a scope exits — through normal control flow, an early return, or even an exception unwinding the stack — RAII gives you automatic, exception-safe cleanup without a single explicit `try/finally`-equivalent block. This one idea underlies `std::lock_guard`, every smart pointer, `std::fstream`, `std::vector`'s own memory management, and essentially all correctly-written resource-owning C++ types.

examples.title: A minimal RAII wrapper around a raw resource
examples.explanation: There is no cleanup code visible anywhere in `process()` — that's the entire point. Whether the function returns normally or an exception propagates out of `parseHeader`/`parseBody`, `f`'s destructor is guaranteed to run as the stack unwinds past it, so the file always gets closed exactly once.

examples.title: RAII for a mutex — the pattern behind std::lock_guard
examples.explanation: This is literally what `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>` does internally. Without RAII, you'd need to remember to call `mtx.unlock()` on every exit path of `criticalSection` — including exceptional ones — which is exactly the kind of manual bookkeeping RAII eliminates.

pitfalls: Writing an RAII class but forgetting to delete (or properly implement) its copy constructor/assignment — a naive memberwise copy of a resource-owning object (e.g. copying `fp` in FileHandle above) leads to two objects both believing they own — and will both try to close/free — the same resource.

Allocating a resource in a constructor that can partially fail (acquiring resource A, then throwing while acquiring resource B) without unwinding what was already acquired — the destructor never runs for an object whose constructor didn't finish, so any RAII sub-members must each independently be exception-safe.
concepts.why: RAII isn't usually asked about directly by name as often as it's ASSUMED — interviewers expect you to reach for it (smart pointers, lock_guard) automatically when discussing resource management, and will probe if you reach for manual malloc/free or lock/unlock instead.

concepts.intro: **Rule of Three** (the pre-C++11 guideline): if a class needs a custom destructor, it's almost certainly managing a resource directly — and if so, it needs a custom copy constructor and copy-assignment operator too, because the compiler-generated memberwise versions would copy the raw resource handle, not the resource itself (see RAII pitfalls above). **Rule of Five** extends this for C++11+: add a move constructor and move-assignment operator too, so the resource can be transferred cheaply instead of always being deep-copied. **Rule of Zero** is the modern preferred design: don't write ANY of the five special members by hand at all — instead, compose your class out of members that ALREADY manage their own resources correctly (std::vector, std::string, std::unique_ptr, etc.), so the compiler-generated defaults for all five special members are automatically correct, because they just recursively do the right thing member-by-member.

examples.title: Rule of Five: a class that legitimately needs all five
examples.explanation: Buffer IS the resource-owning primitive here (it directly holds a raw `int*`), so it must define all five to behave correctly under copying, moving, and destruction — this is exactly the situation where Rule of Five applies.

examples.title: Rule of Zero: the same functionality, none of the boilerplate
examples.explanation: By delegating actual ownership to `std::vector`, Buffer no longer needs to know anything about copying, moving, or freeing memory itself — it inherits correct behavior for free. This is why Rule of Zero is the default modern recommendation: write Rule of Five code only when you're building the resource-owning primitive itself (rare), and Rule of Zero everywhere else (common).

pitfalls: Defining only SOME of the five (e.g. just a destructor, forgetting copy/move) — this is worse than defining none, because it silently disables move operations (the compiler won't generate a move constructor for a class that has a user-declared destructor) and falls back to copying, or worse leaves a raw-resource class with a compiler-generated copy that double-frees.

Writing Rule-of-Five boilerplate for a class that doesn't need it — if your class's members are all well-behaved RAII types already, hand-writing the five special members is pure risk (a bug in hand-rolled boilerplate) for zero benefit over Rule of Zero.

concepts.intro: The three standard smart pointers encode three DIFFERENT ownership philosophies, and picking the wrong one for the situation is a common design-review flag. `std::unique_ptr<T>` is sole ownership: exactly one owner at a time, move-only (copying is disabled), and — crucially — zero runtime overhead over a raw pointer; the object is destroyed the instant the owning unique_ptr goes out of scope. `std::shared_ptr<T>` is shared ownership via ATOMIC reference counting: any number of shared_ptrs can co-own the same object, which is destroyed when the last one goes away — but that shared refcount means copying a shared_ptr is not free (an atomic increment/decrement every time). `std::weak_ptr<T>` observes an object owned by a shared_ptr WITHOUT extending its lifetime or touching the strong refcount — used to break reference cycles and to safely ask "is this thing still alive?" before trying to use it.

examples.title: All three, and when each is the right call
examples.explanation: The cache holding a weak_ptr instead of a shared_ptr is the key design decision here: if the cache held a shared_ptr, it would itself keep every cached Book alive forever, defeating the point of a cache. weak_ptr::lock() is the safe way to attempt access without accidentally extending an object's lifetime.

examples.title: The classic shared_ptr cycle leak
examples.explanation: This is why doubly-linked structures built on shared_ptr deliberately make one direction (commonly "prev"/"parent") a weak_ptr — otherwise the mutual ownership means neither object's reference count ever drops to zero, and both leak silently for the rest of the program's life.

pitfalls: Defaulting to shared_ptr everywhere "to be safe" — this hides ownership intent (who's really responsible for this object?) and pays for atomic refcounting you usually don't need; prefer unique_ptr (or even a plain reference/raw pointer with clear, non-owning semantics) unless shared ownership is a genuine requirement.

Creating a reference cycle with shared_ptrs in both directions of a graph/tree-like structure (see example above) — a very common, very real memory leak in production code, not just an academic gotcha.

Using shared_ptr on a genuinely latency-sensitive hot path without accounting for the atomic increment/decrement cost on every copy — this is a real, measurable cost interviewers expect you to know about.
concepts.why: Extremely commonly asked, often phrased as "implement a basic shared_ptr" or "what happens if two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other" — both of which test whether you understand the reference-counting mechanism, not just the API.

concepts.intro: Every STL container is actually a template over an `Allocator` type (defaulting to one that calls `operator new`/`operator delete`), which is the hook that lets you plug in a custom memory strategy — most commonly, a pre-sized arena or pool allocator — instead of the general-purpose heap for every single allocation. This matters a great deal in latency-sensitive code: the default heap allocator is a general-purpose tool that has to handle arbitrary sizes and frees in arbitrary order, which usually means internal locking and bookkeeping with latency that isn't tightly bounded. A pre-allocated arena, sized for a known maximum number of objects up front, can hand out and reclaim fixed-size chunks in O(1) with no lock contention and no unpredictable tail latency.

examples.title: The shape of a minimal fixed-size pool allocator
examples.explanation: All the storage for up to N objects is claimed once, up front, as a single contiguous block. allocate()/deallocate() then become simple array-scan/index operations — no syscalls, no general-purpose allocator bookkeeping, no lock — at the cost of a hard, known-in-advance capacity limit.

examples.title: Why this matters in a trading-system hot path
examples.explanation: The core idea is moving all allocation-related uncertainty to STARTUP time (when it doesn't matter), so the actual trading-hours hot path never has to ask the OS/general allocator for memory at all.

pitfalls: Assuming a custom allocator automatically makes code thread-safe — a pool allocator shared across threads still needs its own synchronization (or a per-thread pool) unless it's specifically designed to be lock-free.

Over-engineering with a custom allocator before profiling shows the default allocator is actually a bottleneck — this is real complexity/bug-surface you're taking on, and it should be justified by a measured problem, not applied preemptively everywhere.

concepts.intro: A class hides its private implementation details behind a single pointer to a forward-declared struct/class whose full definition lives only in the .cpp file, never the header. The immediate payoff: changing a private member no longer changes the public class's size or forces every translation unit that includes its header to recompile — you're trading one extra heap allocation and one extra pointer indirection per access for dramatically better compile-time isolation (and, as a bonus, a more stable binary interface/ABI, since the public class's memory layout doesn't change when private internals do).

examples.title: The header — completely decoupled from Widget's real internals
examples.explanation: Anyone who includes widget.h sees none of Widget's actual private data members — only a forward-declared Impl and a pointer to it. Adding, removing, or resizing private fields inside Impl never touches this header, so it never forces a rebuild of every file that includes widget.h.

examples.title: The .cpp — where Impl actually lives
examples.explanation: The destructor (and any special member relying on Impl being complete, like the defaulted move operations) has to be DEFINED in the .cpp file, not just declared in the header — see the pitfall below for why getting this wrong is a classic compile error.

pitfalls: Declaring `~Widget()` in the header but letting it be implicitly defined there (or writing `= default` right in the header) — at that point in the header, `Impl` is only forward-declared (incomplete), so `std::unique_ptr<Impl>`'s destructor can't be instantiated; this produces a real, sometimes-confusing compile error about an incomplete type. The fix is always to declare the destructor in the header but DEFINE it (even as `= default`) in the .cpp, after Impl's full definition is visible.

Using PImpl reflexively on every class "for good practice" — it adds a real heap allocation and indirection cost to every object; it's most valuable for classes with either large/frequently-changing private internals or genuine ABI-stability requirements, not as a universal default.

concepts.intro: Three standard levels describe what a piece of code promises will still be true if an exception is thrown partway through it. The **basic guarantee**: no resources leak and the object's invariants still hold, but its exact observable state afterward is unspecified. The **strong guarantee**: the operation either fully succeeds, or has NO visible effect at all — as if it never started (commit-or-rollback semantics) — commonly implemented via the copy-and-swap idiom. The **nothrow (no-throw) guarantee**: the operation is guaranteed to never throw at all, which the standard library actually RELIES on in specific places — most importantly, containers only use a type's move constructor during reallocation if that move constructor is `noexcept`; otherwise they fall back to copying to preserve their own strong guarantee (see Move semantics).

examples.title: The strong guarantee via copy-and-swap
examples.explanation: If step (1)'s copy throws (e.g. out of memory), `*this` has not been modified at all yet — the strong guarantee holds. Step (2), the only part that actually mutates `*this`, is a non-throwing swap, so once you reach it, success is guaranteed. This pattern — build the new state fully off to the side, then commit via a non-throwing swap — is the standard recipe for the strong guarantee.

examples.title: Why noexcept on move operations isn't just documentation
examples.explanation: This is a direct, practical consequence of the nothrow guarantee concept: the standard library's own exception-safety promises are the reason it inspects your type's noexcept-ness before deciding how to treat it internally.

pitfalls: Assuming "basic guarantee" means "nothing bad happens" — it specifically does NOT promise the object's state is predictable afterward, only that it's still valid (destructible, assignable) and nothing leaked. Code relying on a specific post-exception state needs the strong guarantee, not just the basic one.

Forgetting that destructors, swap, and move operations are all expected to provide the no-throw guarantee by convention (and are `noexcept` by default for destructors since C++11) — throwing from any of these is either outright disallowed (destructors during unwinding call std::terminate) or defeats optimizations the standard library specifically makes conditional on noexcept-ness.
